title: What Does Our List of the Best No. 2 Hits Say About What a No. 2 Hit Means — And Does It Still Mean the Same Thing Today? Greatest Pop Stars Podcast
summary: This 'Greatest Pop Stars' podcast episode looks at our staff's recently published 100 Best No. 2 Hits list.
contentText:
All week on Billboard.com, we’ve been celebrating the canon of No. 2 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 — the songs that came as close as they could to ruling the chart, but for one reason or another couldn’t quite make that final leap. On Tuesday (Aug. 11), we published a list of our staff’s 100 favorite such hits , including some signature hits by some of the greatest hitmakers in chart history, as well as some songs that serve as their respective artists’ lone legacy, and plenty of songs in between that we’ve loved for decades, and best capture to us what a No. 2 hit is and should be.

On this week’s episode of the Greatest Pop Stars podcast , we discuss the art of the No. 2 hit, and whether there is something meaningful or maybe even a little mystical to peaking at the runner-up spot on the chart. Host Andrew Unterberger is joined by regular guest Eric Frankenberg of the Billboard charts team to break down the top 10 of our list, as well as sharing some personal picks for songs that could have stood to be a little higher or lower on the list — or that should’ve made the list at all, or not — as well as some favorite No. 2-related quirks in chart history.

Along the way, we discuss all the most pressing questions about No. 2 hits: Does Queen’s “Bohemian Rhapsody” feel more or less like an appropriately representative No. 2 hit for the fact that it took 17 years to get there? Is it a poetically brutal insult for a song to finish second on a list of the best No. 2 hits — or somehow the ultimate compliment? When did “Purple Rain” become the most celebrated Prince hit? How did the Ronettes’ “Be My Baby” get held at No. 2 by a song virtually no one remembers? Should Christina Aguilera’s “Beautiful” get more credit as an all-timer? Do we actually care about the Village People’s “Y.M.C.A.” as a song? And perhaps most importantly: Does a No. 2 hit still mean the same thing it used to, when such hits are less automatically ubiquitous than they used to be, and when pushing a song that final top spot up the chart seems more achievable for properly motivated artists than ever?
